promises.title: Introduce legislation to support and enhance security cooperation, especially within the sub-region and the African continent.
promises.promise_blog:
Nigeria’s security challenges have grown increasingly complex over the last decade, stretching far beyond the country’s borders and revealing the limits of isolated national responses. From insurgency in the Lake Chad Basin to the cross-border movement of small arms, kidnapping networks, human trafficking rings, and the persistent instability along the Sahel corridor, it has become impossible to address insecurity without acknowledging its regional dimensions. The actors driving these threats do not recognize territorial boundaries, yet the institutions responsible for confronting them remain largely national, under-coordinated, and sometimes constrained by outdated laws that do not reflect the realities of modern security dynamics.

 

The significance of strengthening the legal basis for regional security cooperation goes far beyond diplomatic symbolism. It acknowledges that Nigeria’s safety is tied to the stability of its neighbors and that peace in the region is a shared responsibility requiring shared structures. A modern legislative framework would make cooperation predictable rather than ad hoc. It would clarify mandates, reduce bureaucratic delays, improve the interoperability of security agencies, and ensure that partnerships—whether with ECOWAS, the African Union, or bilateral neighbors—are backed by clear legal authority. This is particularly important in an era where violent extremist groups exploit jurisdictional gaps and where technological advances demand more sophisticated, coordinated responses.

 

If the Senate delivers on this promise, the impact could reshape both Nigeria’s security posture and its role on the continent. A stronger legal framework for cooperation would improve real-time intelligence exchange, enhance joint military operations, and facilitate coordinated border management that curtails arms flows and criminal networks. It would expand Nigeria’s influence in regional peacekeeping initiatives and strengthen the country’s leadership in shaping security norms across West Africa. Beyond operational benefits, such legislation would also help rebuild citizen trust by signaling that the government understands the multidimensional nature of insecurity and is committed to solutions that match its scale.

 

In a region where one country’s instability quickly becomes everyone’s problem, acting alone is no longer an option. By modernizing and deepening its legal commitment to regional security cooperation, the Senate has an opportunity to address some of the most persistent threats facing Nigeria and its neighbors. It is a step toward a more secure, more integrated, and more resilient West Africa and a recognition that true security is built not at the borders, but through collective strength and shared resolve.
promises.description: Introduce legislation to support and enhance security cooperation, especially within the sub-region and the African continent.

promises.title: Enact a law that promotes the education of children with special needs, ensuring they have access to quality education in inclusive settings.
promises.promise_blog:
Nigeria’s struggle to provide inclusive education for children with special needs is one of the quietest but most persistent governance failures in the country. For decades, families have navigated a system that was never designed with their children in mind. Schools often lack trained teachers, assistive learning devices, accessible classrooms, or even the basic understanding required to support children who learn and communicate differently. In many communities, these children are kept at home—not because parents do not value education, but because the system offers no meaningful space for them. This has created a cycle where disability and exclusion reinforce each other, limiting opportunities and deepening inequality.

It is against this backdrop that the Senate’s commitment to enact a law promoting quality education for children with special needs becomes profoundly significant. This is not just another education reform; it is a direct challenge to a long-ignored gap in Nigeria’s social contract. At its core, the promise recognizes that a nation cannot claim to value education if its most vulnerable learners are left at the margins. It acknowledges that inclusive education is not charity—it is a matter of rights, dignity, and national development. When children with disabilities are denied access to learning, the country loses potential teachers, innovators, voters, workers, and leaders. When they are included, society grows stronger, more compassionate, and more productive.

The governance challenge here is substantial. Inclusive education requires more than building ramps or printing new policies. It demands a legal framework that compels states, schools, and institutions to adapt their systems, train educators, fund specialized support services, and monitor compliance. It requires shifting mindsets in a country where disability is still surrounded by stigma and misunderstanding. Without clear laws and strong enforcement, the gaps will persist, children will continue to be turned away, and families will continue to bear the burden alone.

Impact:

fulfilling this legislative promise could be transformative. A well-crafted law could guarantee that every child with special needs has the right to learn in an environment where they are not merely accommodated but genuinely included. It could ensure that teachers are trained to understand diverse learning needs, that schools are equipped to support them, and that discrimination is not just frowned upon but legally punishable. Such a law could open classrooms that have remained closed for generations and send a message that every child, regardless of ability, has something to contribute to the nation’s future.

By taking this step, the Senate has an opportunity to redefine what fairness and justice look like in Nigeria’s education system. Delivering on this promise would not only change the lives of thousands of children; it would reshape the country’s moral architecture proving that progress is measured not by how a nation treats its strongest, but how it uplifts those who need support the most.
promises.description: Enact a law that promotes the education of children with special needs, ensuring they have access to quality education in inclusive settings.

promises.title: Revise and strengthen the Nigerian Ports Authority (NPA) Act, ensuring it has a clear mandate, authority, and resources to efficiently manage and develop the ports
promises.promise_blog:
Nigeria’s ports sit at the heart of its economy, yet for decades the legal and institutional framework governing them has been out of sync with the scale and complexity of modern maritime trade. The Nigerian Ports Authority, once envisioned as the country’s gateway for commerce, job creation, and industrial growth, now operates under an outdated Act that no longer reflects the realities of global logistics, private-sector participation, digital operations, or the rapidly expanding demands of regional trade. The result is a system marked by chronic congestion, bureaucratic overlaps, slow cargo processing, and infrastructure that has struggled to keep pace with rising volumes of imports and exports.

 

This is the underlying governance challenge that drives the Senate’s commitment to revise and strengthen the NPA Act. The current law leaves too much ambiguity around the Authority’s mandate, blurring the lines between regulation and operation, complicating coordination among agencies, and limiting the NPA’s ability to take swift decisions that improve efficiency. Without a clear legal foundation, the port system becomes vulnerable to administrative bottlenecks, political interference, revenue leakages, and fragmented responsibilities that cost the country billions in lost trade opportunities and logistics inefficiencies. At a time when global ports are moving toward automation, multilayered security systems, and 24-hour integrated operations, Nigeria cannot continue relying on an outdated legal framework that slows progress rather than enabling it.

 

The significance of revising the NPA Act goes beyond improving cargo movement. It is fundamentally about restoring Nigeria’s position as a competitive maritime hub in West Africa. Ports are not just warehouses for goods they are strategic national assets that shape industrialization, foreign investment, and regional influence. When the NPA has clear authority, adequate resources, and a modern mandate, it can drive reforms that cut down turnaround times, modernize port infrastructure, improve security, and create a transparent environment that boosts investor confidence. A strong law would also clarify the roles of agencies operating at the ports, reducing duplication and turf wars that have historically undermined performance.

 

Delivering on this legislative promise could have a transformative impact on the economy. Efficient ports lower the cost of doing business, make Nigerian exports more competitive, and help manufacturers access raw materials more quickly. It would also enhance revenue generation, reduce corruption-prone manual processes, and address long-standing delays that discourage global shipping companies from making Nigeria a preferred destination. Stronger port governance would support the growth of special economic zones, stimulate job creation across the logistics value chain, and improve the ease of doing business at a scale that affects every sector from agriculture to pharmaceuticals to technology.
promises.description: Revise and strengthen the Nigerian Ports Authority (NPA) Act, ensuring it has a clear mandate, authority, and resources to efficiently manage and develop the ports

promises.title: Amendments to the Universal Basic Education (UBEC) Act that mandates free and compulsory education to Senior Secondary School
promises.promise_blog:
Nigeria’s education system has long struggled under the weight of uneven access, chronic underfunding, and policy gaps that leave millions of children behind. While the Universal Basic Education (UBE) framework was a major step toward guaranteeing free and compulsory schooling, its coverage stops at Junior Secondary School, creating a structural break that has quietly undermined the country’s ambition of building an educated and competitive population. For many families, especially in rural and low-income communities, this policy gap is the difference between a child completing secondary education and dropping out prematurely. The transition from Junior to Senior Secondary School becomes a financial hurdle many simply cannot cross.

The significance of amending the UBEC Act lies in its potential to redefine the scope of Nigeria’s commitment to human capital development. A clear legal extension of free and compulsory education would force a long-overdue alignment between national aspirations and actual policy infrastructure. It would compel federal and state governments to rethink funding models, teacher recruitment, infrastructure investment, and quality assurance mechanisms for Senior Secondary education. It would also send a strong signal to parents and communities that the state is prepared to shoulder its responsibility for educating children beyond basic literacy.

The impact of such a reform could be profound. With millions more teenagers staying in school, Nigeria would experience measurable improvements in literacy, workforce readiness, and long-term economic productivity. Students would gain stronger foundations in science, technology, vocational skills, and civic education preparing them for either higher education or skilled employment. Extending free Senior Secondary education would also strengthen gender equality by reducing dropout rates among adolescent girls and protecting them from early marriage and exploitation.

More broadly, this amendment could reshape the country’s development trajectory. A nation that ensures its young people are educated to at least Senior Secondary level becomes more secure, more prosperous, and better equipped to compete globally. By expanding the scope of compulsory education, the Senate has the opportunity to fix one of the quiet but consequential gaps in Nigeria’s policy landscape: a reform that could influence not only individual futures, but the country’s collective destiny for generations.
promises.description: Amendments to the Universal Basic Education (UBEC) Act that mandates free and compulsory education to Senior Secondary School
